The optimal reverse noise is locked to the state's own fluctuation geometry and simultaneously minimizes the geometric, metrological, and thermodynamic price of reversal. For multimode trajectories, the exact cost is additive in a canonical set of mode-resolved data, and a globally continuous protocol attains this optimum on every mixed-state interval. If a pure nonclassical endpoint is included, the same pointwise law holds for every $t>0$, but the optimum diverges as $2/t$: exact reversal of a pure quantum state is dynamically unattainable. These results establish an exact law of quantum reversibility in the canonical pure-loss setting and provide a sharp benchmark for broader theories of quantum reverse diffusion.

AI.tldr: Quantum reverse diffusion for Gaussian pure-loss dynamics exhibits an exact phase boundary where minimum reverse cost vanishes at critical squeezing-to-thermal ratio, with sharp asymmetry and singular behavior for pure nonclassical states.
AI.motivation: To establish an exact law of quantum reversibility in the canonical pure-loss setting (Gaussian pure-loss dynamics) that governs continuous-variable decoherence in optical attenuation channels, squeezed-light interferometric sensing, and superconducting bosonic architectures.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum reverse diffusion under complete positivity constraints, examining the phase boundary behavior, reverse-noise budget, and optimal reverse protocols including covariance-aligned generator and globally continuous protocols for multimode trajectories.
AI.result: Exact phase boundary at critical squeezing-to-thermal ratio where minimum reverse cost vanishes; sharp asymmetry with standard reverse prescriptions feasible below boundary but infeasible above; pure nonclassical targets are dynamically singular with exact reversal unattainable (cost diverges as 2/t).
AI.conclusion: Establishes an exact law of quantum reversibility for Gaussian pure-loss dynamics, providing a sharp benchmark for broader theories of quantum reverse diffusion and revealing fundamental limitations in reversing pure quantum states.

title: Fair Decoder Baselines and Rigorous Finite-Size Scaling for Bivariate Bicycle Codes on the Quantum Erasure Channel
summary: Fair threshold estimation for bivariate bicycle (BB) codes on the quantum erasure channel runs into two recurring problems: decoder-baseline unfairness and the conflation of finite-size pseudo-thresholds with true asymptotic thresholds. We run both uninformed and \emph{erasure-aware} minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) surface code baselines alongside BP-OSD decoding of BB codes. With standard depolarizing-weight MWPM and no erasure information, performance matches random guessing on the erasure channel in our tested regime -- so prior work that compares against this baseline is really comparing decoders, not codes. Using 200{,}000 shots per point and bootstrap confidence intervals, we sweep five BB code sizes from $N=144$ to $N=1296$. Pseudo-thresholds (WER = 0.10) run from $p^* = 0.370$ to $0.471$; finite-size scaling (FSS) gives an asymptotic threshold $p^*_\infty \approx 0.488$, within 2.4\% of the zero-rate limit and without maximum-likelihood decoding. On the fair baseline, BB at $N=1296$ has a modest edge in threshold over the surface code at twice the qubit count, and a 12$\times$ lower normalized overhead -- the latter is where the practical advantage sits. All runs are reproducible from recorded seeds and package versions.

AI.tldr: BB codes show modest threshold advantage over surface codes on quantum erasure channel with 12× lower normalized overhead, achieving asymptotic threshold p*∞ ≈ 0.488 without maximum-likelihood decoding.
AI.motivation: Address two recurring problems in fair threshold estimation for BB codes: decoder-baseline unfairness and conflation of finite-size pseudo-thresholds with true asymptotic thresholds on quantum erasure channel.
AI.method: Compare both uninformed and erasure-aware MWPM surface code baselines alongside BP-OSD decoding of BB codes. Use 200,000 shots per point with bootstrap confidence intervals, sweeping five BB code sizes from N=144 to N=1296. Employ finite-size scaling for asymptotic threshold estimation.
AI.result: Pseudo-thresholds (WER=0.10) range from p* = 0.370 to 0.471; finite-size scaling gives asymptotic threshold p*∞ ≈ 0.488, within 2.4% of zero-rate limit. BB at N=1296 shows modest threshold edge over surface code at twice qubit count with 12× lower normalized overhead.
AI.conclusion: BB codes offer practical advantage through significantly lower normalized overhead (12× reduction) rather than dramatic threshold improvements, with fair baseline comparisons showing prior work conflated decoder performance with code performance.

title: Photon-echo synchronization and quantum state transfer in short quantum links
summary: The short quantum link regime, where the photon travel time $τ$ is comparable to the emitter lifetime $1/γ$, is experimentally relevant but theoretically underexplored: existing few-mode descriptions lose validity as retardation and multimode effects become significant. Using a Delay Differential Equation (DDE) framework that admits exact analytical solutions from the single-mode cavity limit to the multimode waveguide continuum, we show that emitters coupled to a short link spontaneously lock into self-synchronized Rabi oscillations driven by coherent photon echoes, breaking the link's discrete time-displacement symmetry. The resulting spectral structure -- persistent quasi-dark states and vacuum Rabi splitting, including in the superstrong coupling regime -- enables efficient quantum state transfer (QST): benchmarking three protocols across the full $γτ$ parameter space, we find that STIRAP exploits the quasi-dark-state structure to achieve a quadratic infidelity floor $\mathcal{O}((γτ)^2)$, outperforming both SWAP (linear error $\mathcal{O}(γτ)$) and wavepacket engineering for $γτ\lesssim 1.44$, even in regimes where retardation cannot be neglected. These results establish photon-echo synchronization as an engineering resource for quantum state transfer, with DDE modeling providing the exact analytical predictions needed to design and optimize short-link experiments on current circuit-QED hardware.

AI.tldr: Short quantum links (photon travel time comparable to emitter lifetime) enable self-synchronized Rabi oscillations via photon echoes, breaking time-displacement symmetry and creating quasi-dark states that enhance quantum state transfer efficiency.
AI.motivation: The short quantum link regime (τ ~ 1/γ) is experimentally relevant but theoretically underexplored, as existing few-mode descriptions fail when retardation and multimode effects become significant. Current theoretical frameworks lose validity in this regime.
AI.method: Developed a Delay Differential Equation (DDE) framework that provides exact analytical solutions spanning from single-mode cavity limit to multimode waveguide continuum. Used this to analyze emitter dynamics and benchmark three quantum state transfer protocols (STIRAP, SWAP, wavepacket engineering) across the full γτ parameter space.
AI.result: Emitters coupled to short links spontaneously lock into self-synchronized Rabi oscillations driven by coherent photon echoes, breaking discrete time-displacement symmetry. This creates persistent quasi-dark states and vacuum Rabi splitting, even in superstrong coupling. STIRAP exploits quasi-dark-state structure to achieve quadratic infidelity floor O((γτ)²), outperforming SWAP (linear error O(γτ)) and wavepacket engineering for γτ ≲ 1.44.
AI.conclusion: Photon-echo synchronization serves as an engineering resource for quantum state transfer. The DDE modeling provides exact analytical predictions needed to design and optimize short-link experiments on current circuit-QED hardware, establishing a framework for exploiting retardation effects rather than treating them as limitations.

title: Utility-scale quantum computational chemistry
summary: Chemistry and materials science are widely regarded as potential killer application fields for quantum hardware. While the dream of unlocking unprecedented simulation capabilities remains compelling, quantum algorithm development must adapt to the evolving constraints of the emerging quantum hardware in order to accomplish any advantage for the computational chemistry practice. At the same time, the continuous advancement of classical wavefunction-theory methods narrows the window for a broad quantum advantage. Here, we explore potential benefits of quantum computation from the broader perspective of utility-scale applications. We argue that quantum algorithms need not only enable accurate calculations for a few challenging, that is strongly correlated, molecular structures, that might be hard to describe with traditional methods. Instead, they must also support the practical integration of quantum-accelerated computations into high-throughput pipelines for routine calculations on arbitrary molecules, ultimately delivering a tangible value to society.

AI.tldr: Quantum computing for chemistry must adapt to hardware constraints and integrate into practical workflows to deliver societal value, not just solve strongly correlated problems.
AI.motivation: While quantum computing holds promise for chemistry and materials science, quantum algorithms must evolve to match emerging hardware constraints and compete with advancing classical methods to achieve practical advantage.
AI.method: The paper takes a broader perspective on utility-scale applications, arguing that quantum algorithms should support integration into high-throughput pipelines for routine calculations on arbitrary molecules rather than just focusing on strongly correlated systems.
AI.result: The analysis suggests that quantum advantage in chemistry requires not only accurate calculations for challenging molecular structures but also practical integration into computational workflows that deliver tangible societal value.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing for chemistry must shift focus from solving isolated strongly correlated problems to developing algorithms that can be practically integrated into high-throughput computational pipelines to achieve meaningful societal impact.

title: Practical Quantum Broadcasting
comment: 6 pages (main text) + 58 pages (supplemental material), packed with extensive figures and illustrations. Comments welcome!
summary: Incorporating sample efficiency, by requiring the number of states consumed by broadcasting does not exceed that of a naive prepare-and-distribute strategy, gives rise to the no practical quantum broadcasting theorem. To navigate this limitation, we introduce approximate and probabilistic virtual broadcasting and derive analytic expressions for their optimal sample complexity overheads. Allowing deviations at the receivers restores sample efficiency even in the 1-to-2 approximate setting, whereas probabilistic protocols obey a stronger no-go theorem that excludes all sample efficient 1-to-2 implementations for arbitrary dimension and success probability. Rather counterintuitive, this obstruction does not persist at larger receiver numbers: for qubit systems, practical 1-to-6 virtual broadcasting becomes attainable. These results elevate sample complexity from a technical constraint to a defining operational principle, opening an unexplored route to the efficient distribution of quantum information.

AI.tldr: No-go theorem for practical quantum broadcasting with sample efficiency constraints; introduces approximate/probabilistic virtual broadcasting with analytic sample complexity overheads; shows surprising dimension-dependent feasibility for multi-receiver scenarios.
AI.motivation: To address the fundamental limitation of quantum broadcasting under sample efficiency constraints, where traditional prepare-and-distribute strategies set a benchmark for state consumption.
AI.method: Introduces approximate and probabilistic virtual broadcasting protocols, derives analytic expressions for optimal sample complexity overheads, and analyzes feasibility across different receiver numbers and dimensions.
AI.result: Approximate broadcasting allows sample-efficient 1-to-2 implementations with receiver deviations, while probabilistic protocols obey a stronger no-go theorem excluding all sample-efficient 1-to-2 implementations. Surprisingly, practical 1-to-6 virtual broadcasting becomes attainable for qubit systems.
AI.conclusion: Sample complexity emerges as a defining operational principle rather than just a technical constraint, opening new routes for efficient quantum information distribution with dimension-dependent feasibility thresholds.

title: Active Quantum Particles from Engineered Dissipation
summary: We introduce and characterize different models for an active quantum particle where activity arises from engineered dissipation-- specifically, from a suitably coupled nonequilibrium environment. These include a model of a particle moving on a lattice with coherent and dissipative hopping, as well as quantum generalizations of well-studied models of active behavior, such as the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, run-and-tumble dynamics, and the active Brownian particle. Despite the different microscopic mechanisms at play, we show that all these models display key features of active motion. Notably, we observe a crossover from diffusive to active-diffusive behavior at long times, leading to an effective Péclet number, as well as a strong sensitivity to boundary conditions which, in our open quantum system context, arises from the Liouville skin effect. We discuss the role of quantum fluctuations and experimental realizations with superconducting circuits or cold gases, closing with perspectives for many-body effects in quantum active matter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum models of active particles driven by engineered dissipation, showing they exhibit key active matter features like diffusive-to-active-diffusive crossover and boundary sensitivity from the Liouville skin effect.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum models of active matter where activity arises from engineered dissipation rather than biological or chemical processes, bridging nonequilibrium quantum systems with active matter physics.
AI.method: Introduces several quantum active particle models including lattice models with coherent/dissipative hopping, quantum generalizations of classical active models (active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, run-and-tumble, active Brownian particle), and analyzes them using open quantum system approaches.
AI.result: All models display key active matter features: crossover from diffusive to active-diffusive behavior at long times with effective Péclet number, strong boundary condition sensitivity arising from Liouville skin effect in open quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: Engineered dissipation can create quantum active matter with characteristic active motion features, opening possibilities for experimental realization in superconducting circuits or cold gases and exploration of many-body quantum active matter.

title: Entanglement assisted communication complexity measured by distinguishability
summary: We investigate the quantum advantage that can arise in typical two-party communication scenarios, where the sender and the receiver are allowed to share prior correlations. Focusing on communication tasks constrained by the distinguishability of the sender's inputs, we demonstrate that entanglement-assisted communication, both classical and quantum, can outperform classical communication supplemented with shared randomness. We begin by developing a general framework for communication tasks with pre-shared correlations. We identify certain communication tasks that exhibit an advantage under entanglement assistance compared to classical communication. Through these results, we establish a connection between quantum communication and entanglement-assisted classical communication, and also show an equivalence between entanglement-assisted classical communication and entanglement-assisted quantum communication. We then consider the simplest scenarios in which the receiver has no input and demonstrate that entanglement-assisted strategies still offer advantages over both classical communication and quantum communication without prior entanglement. Finally, by constructing a class of communication tasks, we show that a non-maximally entangled state can, in some cases, be more useful than a maximally entangled state as a pre-shared resource.

AI.tldr: Quantum communication with pre-shared entanglement outperforms classical communication with shared randomness, with non-maximally entangled states sometimes being more useful than maximally entangled ones.
AI.motivation: To investigate quantum advantages in two-party communication scenarios where sender and receiver can share prior correlations, focusing on tasks constrained by input distinguishability and comparing different resource-assisted communication models.
AI.method: Developed a general framework for communication tasks with pre-shared correlations, identified specific tasks showing entanglement advantage, established connections between different communication models, and constructed classes of communication tasks to compare resource effectiveness.
AI.result: Demonstrated that entanglement-assisted communication (both classical and quantum) outperforms classical communication with shared randomness, showed advantages even in simplest scenarios with no receiver input, and proved that non-maximally entangled states can sometimes be more useful than maximally entangled states as pre-shared resources.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantages exist in correlation-assisted communication, with entanglement providing superior performance over classical randomness, and non-maximal entanglement offering unexpected benefits in certain communication tasks.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography from Quantum Stabilizer Decoding
summary: Post-quantum cryptography currently rests on a small number of hardness assumptions, posing significant risks should any one of them be compromised. This vulnerability motivates the search for new and cryptographically versatile assumptions that make a convincing case for quantum hardness. In this work, we argue that decoding random quantum stabilizer codes -- a quantum analog of the well-studied LPN problem -- is an excellent candidate. This task occupies a unique middle ground: it is inherently native to quantum computation, yet admits an equivalent formulation with purely classical input and output, as recently shown by Khesin et al. (STOC '26). We prove that the average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding implies the core primitives of classical Cryptomania, including public-key encryption (PKE) and oblivious transfer (OT), as well as one-way functions. Our constructions are moreover practical: our PKE scheme achieves essentially the same efficiency as state-of-the-art LPN-based PKE, and our OT is round-optimal. We also provide substantial evidence that stabilizer decoding does not reduce to LPN, suggesting that the former problem constitutes a genuinely new post-quantum assumption. Our primary technical contributions are twofold. First, we give a reduction from random quantum stabilizer decoding to an average-case problem closely resembling LPN, but which is equipped with additional symplectic algebraic structure. While this structure is essential to the quantum nature of the problem, it raises significant barriers to cryptographic security reductions. Second, we develop a new suit of scrambling techniques for such structured linear spaces, and use them to produce rigorous security proofs for all of our constructions.

AI.tldr: Quantum stabilizer code decoding is proposed as a new post-quantum hardness assumption enabling practical PKE, OT, and one-way functions with evidence it doesn't reduce to LPN.
AI.motivation: Current post-quantum cryptography relies on few hardness assumptions, creating systemic risk if any are broken. Need new quantum-hard assumptions with cryptographic versatility.
AI.method: 1) Reduce random quantum stabilizer decoding to average-case problem resembling LPN but with symplectic algebraic structure. 2) Develop scrambling techniques for structured linear spaces to enable security proofs. 3) Construct practical PKE and round-optimal OT schemes based on this assumption.
AI.result: Proved average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding implies classical Cryptomania primitives (PKE, OT, one-way functions). PKE efficiency matches state-of-the-art LPN-based schemes. Provided evidence stabilizer decoding doesn't reduce to LPN, suggesting genuinely new assumption.
AI.conclusion: Quantum stabilizer code decoding is a promising new post-quantum hardness assumption that is native to quantum computation yet classically formulable, enabling practical cryptographic constructions with rigorous security proofs.

title: Low-weight quantum syndrome errors in belief propagation decoding
summary: We describe an empirical approach to identify low-weight combinations of columns of the decoding matrices of a quantum circuit-level noise model, for which belief-propagation (BP) algorithms converge possibly very slowly. Focusing on the logical-idle syndrome cycle of the low-density parity check gross code, we identify criteria providing a characterization of the Tanner subgraph of such low-weight error syndromes. We analyze the dynamics of iterations when BP is used to decode weight-four and weight-five errors, finding statistics akin to exponential activation in the presence of noise or escape from chaotic phase-space domains. We study how BP convergence improves when adding to the decoding matrix relevant combinations of fault columns, and show that the suggested decoder amendment can result in the reduction of both logical errors and decoding time.

AI.tldr: Empirical identification of low-weight error syndromes causing slow BP convergence in quantum error correction, with decoder amendments improving both logical error rates and decoding time.
AI.motivation: To address slow convergence of belief-propagation (BP) algorithms in quantum error correction by identifying problematic low-weight error syndromes in quantum circuit-level noise models.
AI.method: Empirical approach to identify low-weight combinations of columns in decoding matrices where BP converges slowly; analysis of Tanner subgraphs for weight-4 and weight-5 errors; study of BP dynamics with noise; amendment of decoder by adding relevant fault column combinations.
AI.result: Identification of criteria characterizing Tanner subgraphs of low-weight error syndromes; observation of exponential activation dynamics in noisy conditions; demonstration that decoder amendments reduce both logical errors and decoding time.
AI.conclusion: Targeted amendments to decoding matrices based on identified problematic error syndromes can significantly improve BP decoder performance in quantum error correction, enhancing both accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Quantum block encoding for semiseparable matrices
summary:
Quantum block encoding (QBE) is a crucial step in the development of most quantum algorithms, as it provides an embedding of a given matrix into a suitable larger unitary matrix. Historically, the development of efficient techniques for QBE has mostly focused on sparse matrices; less effort has been devoted to data-sparse (e.g., rank-structured) matrices.
  In this work we examine a particular case of rank structure, namely, one-pair semiseparable matrices. We present a new block encoding approach that relies on a suitable factorization of the given matrix as the product of triangular and diagonal factors. To encode the matrix, the algorithm needs $2\log(N)+7$ ancillary qubits. This process takes polylogarithmic time and has an error of $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$, where $N$ is the matrix size.

AI.tldr: Novel quantum block encoding method for one-pair semiseparable matrices using triangular-diagonal factorization with polylogarithmic time and O(N²) error.
AI.motivation: Quantum block encoding development has focused on sparse matrices, with less attention to data-sparse/rank-structured matrices like semiseparable matrices, creating a gap in efficient encoding techniques for this important class.
AI.method: Factorization-based approach decomposing one-pair semiseparable matrices into triangular and diagonal factors, requiring 2log(N)+7 ancillary qubits for encoding.
AI.result: Achieves polylogarithmic time complexity for block encoding with error scaling as O(N²), where N is matrix size, demonstrating efficient encoding for this rank-structured matrix class.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully extends quantum block encoding capabilities to one-pair semiseparable matrices, addressing the gap in efficient encoding techniques for rank-structured matrices beyond sparse matrices.

title: Quantum Structures as Generative Scores: Partition Logic, Generative Logic, and Aesthetic Form
summary: We connect partition logic with Generative Logic by translating finite partition logics into Prolog-based Simple Generative Logic Grammars. As a proof of concept, we use the five-atom V-logic L_{12} to generate a modular visual artifact, the \emph{Quantum Square}. The approach separates logical structure from its visual, textual, or sonic realization. This makes partition logic useful both as a generative design resource and as a tool for communicating complementarity.

AI.tldr: Translation of finite partition logics into Prolog-based Simple Generative Logic Grammars, demonstrated with V-logic L₁₂ to generate a modular visual artifact called the Quantum Square.
AI.motivation: To connect partition logic with generative logic and demonstrate its utility as both a generative design resource and a tool for communicating complementarity concepts.
AI.method: Translate finite partition logics into Prolog-based Simple Generative Logic Grammars, using the five-atom V-logic L₁₂ as a proof of concept to generate the Quantum Square modular visual artifact.
AI.result: Successful generation of the Quantum Square visual artifact, demonstrating that partition logic can be effectively translated into generative grammars for creating modular designs.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully separates logical structure from its realization (visual, textual, or sonic), making partition logic useful for both generative design and communicating complementarity concepts.

title: Measurement-Induced Quantum Neural Network
summary: We introduce a measurement-induced quantum neural network (MINN), an adaptive monitored-circuit architecture in which mid-circuit measurement outcomes determine the entangling gates in subsequent layers. In contrast to standard monitored circuits where sites and gates are sampled randomly, the gates are parametrized and variational, producing correlated history-dependent dynamics and injecting nonlinearity through measurement back-action. A generic MINN is not expected to be efficiently classically simulable. To demonstrate feasibility, we study a matchgate MINN that admits exact fermionic simulation and can be trained with gradient estimators. We apply the architecture to continuous optimization, image classification, and ground-state search in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, finding effective training and performance over a broad range of monitoring rates.

AI.tldr: MINN is a quantum neural network architecture using measurement outcomes to adaptively control subsequent entangling gates, enabling correlated history-dependent dynamics and measurement-induced nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum neural network architecture that leverages measurement back-action for nonlinearity and adaptive dynamics, overcoming limitations of standard monitored circuits with random sampling.
AI.method: Introduces measurement-induced quantum neural network (MINN) with adaptive monitored-circuit architecture where mid-circuit measurement outcomes determine subsequent entangling gates; uses parametrized variational gates; studies matchgate MINN variant for exact fermionic simulation and gradient-based training.
AI.result: MINN architecture is not expected to be efficiently classically simulable; matchgate MINN variant demonstrates feasibility with exact fermionic simulation and effective training across continuous optimization, image classification, and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass ground-state search over broad monitoring rates.
AI.conclusion: MINN provides a novel quantum neural network framework combining measurement-induced nonlinearity and adaptive dynamics, with demonstrated feasibility through matchgate variant showing effective training and performance across diverse tasks.

title: Quantum theory based on real numbers cannot be experimentally falsified
comment: 60 pages (7 main, 10 technical material, 43 appendices), 5 figures (4 in main, 1 in appendix)
summary: Whether the complex numbers of standard quantum theory are experimentally indispensable has remained open for decades. Real quantum theory (RQT), obtained by replacing complex amplitudes with real ones while retaining the usual Kronecker-product composition rule, reproduces all single-party and bipartite Bell correlations of quantum theory (QT), but its lack of local tomography suggested that the two theories might diverge in more general local experiments. This possibility appeared to be confirmed by Renou et al., who argued that a bilocal network experiment can falsify RQT without falsifying QT. Here we show that this conclusion relies on an experimentally untestable assumption. The key distinction is between product-state independence, which constrains the mathematical form of source states, and operational independence, which is defined entirely by the absence of observable cross-source correlations. We prove that, once source independence is imposed operationally, every finite network correlation achievable in QT is also achievable in RQT with the same locality structure of the measurements. We then extend this equivalence to arbitrary finite sequential multipartite protocols involving channels and measurements with prescribed locality structure. Thus, as long as no violation of QT is observed, RQT cannot be experimentally falsified. Our results restore the empirical indistinguishability of QT and RQT, while showing that they support markedly different pictures of the correlation structure underlying the same observed world.

AI.tldr: Real quantum theory (RQT) is empirically indistinguishable from standard quantum theory (QT) in all finite network and sequential protocols when source independence is imposed operationally rather than as product-state independence.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing question of whether complex numbers in quantum theory are experimentally indispensable by examining whether real quantum theory (RQT) can be experimentally distinguished from standard quantum theory (QT) in network scenarios.
AI.method: Distinguish between product-state independence (mathematical form constraint) and operational independence (absence of observable cross-source correlations). Prove that with operational independence, every finite network correlation achievable in QT is also achievable in RQT with the same measurement locality structure. Extend this equivalence to arbitrary finite sequential multipartite protocols involving channels and measurements.
AI.result: RQT cannot be experimentally falsified as long as no violation of QT is observed. The two theories are empirically indistinguishable while supporting different pictures of the underlying correlation structure.
AI.conclusion: Complex numbers in standard quantum theory are not experimentally indispensable; RQT and QT are empirically indistinguishable in all finite network and sequential protocols when source independence is properly operationalized, restoring their empirical equivalence while highlighting their different interpretations of correlation structure.

title: The commutant of fermionic Gaussian unitaries
summary: In this work, we characterize the $t$-th order commutants of fermionic Gaussian unitaries and of their particle-preserving subgroup acting on $n$ fermionic modes. These commutants govern Haar averages over the corresponding groups and therefore play a central role in fermionic randomized protocols, invariant theory, and resource quantification. Using Howe dualities, we show that the particle-preserving commutant is generated by generalized copy-hopping operators, while that for general Gaussian commutant is generated by generalized quadratic Majorana bilinears together with parity. We then derive closed formulas for the dimensions of both commutants as functions of $t$ and $n$, and develop constructive Gelfand--Tsetlin procedures to obtain explicit orthonormal bases, with detailed low-$t$ examples. Our framework also clarifies the structure of replicated fermionic states and connects naturally to measures of fermionic correlations, generalized Plücker-type constraints, and the stabilizer entropy of fermionic Gaussian states. These results provide a unified algebraic description of higher-order invariants for fermionic Gaussian dynamics.

AI.tldr: Characterization of t-th order commutants for fermionic Gaussian unitaries and their particle-preserving subgroup, providing algebraic foundations for fermionic randomized protocols and invariant theory.
AI.motivation: Commutants govern Haar averages over fermionic groups and play central roles in fermionic randomized protocols, invariant theory, and resource quantification, necessitating systematic characterization.
AI.method: Using Howe dualities to analyze commutants, showing particle-preserving commutant generated by generalized copy-hopping operators, general Gaussian commutant by generalized quadratic Majorana bilinears plus parity, deriving dimension formulas, and developing Gelfand-Tsetlin procedures for explicit bases.
AI.result: Closed formulas for dimensions of both commutants as functions of t and n, constructive procedures for orthonormal bases, clarification of replicated fermionic states structure, connections to fermionic correlation measures, generalized Plücker constraints, and stabilizer entropy.
AI.conclusion: Provides unified algebraic description of higher-order invariants for fermionic Gaussian dynamics, establishing foundations for fermionic randomized protocols and resource quantification.
